messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meera was twenty-three when it happened, a bright Tuesday afternoon in late spring. She had just finished a shift at the community counseling center where she worked, and was walking toward the bus stop, her mind still half-occupied with a client’s story. The air smelled of damp earth from a nearby park, and she noticed a police cruiser idling at the corner before she reached the shelter. She barely registered it—she had grown up in this neighborhood, knew its rhythms. Then a second cruiser appeared, and a third, and within seconds officers were converging on a young man near the bus stop. Meera froze. She was not the target, she understood that intellectually, but the sudden violence of the takedown—the shouting, the knees in a spine, the way the man’s face was ground into the concrete—unlocked something in her that she had not known was there. An officer grabbed her arm and shoved her back, telling her to move along, and in that moment her body became a stranger to her. She felt her knees give, then a hand on the back of her neck pushing her down, and for a few seconds she was certain she was going to be arrested or worse. It lasted maybe two minutes. The young man was handcuffed and driven away. Meera was left standing on the sidewalk, shaking, the smell of soil and exhaust thick in her throat.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not behave like a normal memory. Sometimes she could recall the sequence of events with perfect clarity but felt nothing—a hollow, clinical replay, as if she were watching a stranger on a screen. Other times, without warning, the memory would return in full sensory force: the weight of the officer’s hand, the grit of the pavement against her cheek, the smell of earth and sweat, and her body would lock into the same position she had been in, her hands pressed flat against an invisible ground, her breath shallow and fast. These episodes left her disoriented and afraid. She began to avoid the bus altogether, walking the two miles to work even when it rained, because the moment she stepped onto a bus the smell of the floor—that mixture of dirt and rubber—would trigger a full reenactment. She also stopped seeing friends from before the event, people who had known her as easygoing and unafraid. She could not explain to them why she flinched at a raised voice or why she had started covering her face with her hands whenever a police car passed. She felt contaminated by what had happened, as if the dirt on the pavement had seeped into her skin and could not be washed off. She had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that anyone—a neighbor, a client, a stranger on the street—could turn dangerous without warning. This distrust reshaped her world. She began studying faces and body language obsessively, scanning for threat before she could even think about what she was doing. Her body reacted before her mind, and she had learned to trust that physical alarm more than anything else.

The more she scanned, the more she found. A man standing too still at a crosswalk. A woman with her hand in her pocket. Every face held a hidden intention. This vigilance made it impossible to fall asleep at night—she needed to stay alert, to keep watch—and the exhaustion only deepened her sense of estrangement from the world around her. She checked mirrors obsessively, at work and at home, needing to know who was behind her at all times. The mirror-checking became a compulsion that reinforced the very danger she was trying to avoid: each glance confirmed that she was right to be afraid, that the world was full of potential threats. She began to feel that she had lost her connection to her community and culture, the very things that had once made her feel safe in her own skin. She was a counselor, trained to help others process trauma, but she could not process her own. The irony was not lost on her. At work, she found herself scanning clients’ faces for threat instead of listening, and she started canceling sessions with anyone who reminded her of the officers—young men with short hair, anyone in a uniform. The bus remained impossible. She could not ride it without her body going rigid, her hands flying to her face, the memory surging back as if it were happening again in real time. The smell of soil, once a comfort from childhood, now made her nauseous.

What finally brought Meera to seek help was a moment of recognition in the counseling center’s bathroom mirror. She had just finished a session with a client who had described a similar experience—a sudden, violent encounter with police—and Meera had nodded along, offered grounding techniques, felt nothing. Then she locked herself in the stall and pressed her palms against the cold tile, her body reenacting the position she had been forced into two years earlier. She saw her own face in the mirror afterward, hollow and numb, and she thought: I am becoming a stranger to myself. She was terrified that the contamination would never lift, that she would spend the rest of her life scanning faces and checking mirrors and hiding from buses. She was hoping, more than anything, that someone could help her feel clean again.
